utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I hope you are the same Naser Oric we have been seeing for a year and a half. Mr. Oric, can you follow the proceedings in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour, ladies and gentlemen, I can follow the proceedings in my own language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Good morning to you, and you may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, and also good morning to my learned friends of the Defence. My name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution. I am here together with co-counsel, Ms. Patricia Sellers, Mr. Gramsci Di Fazio, and Ms. Joanne Richardson, and our case manager, Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Wubben, and good morning to you and your team. Appearances for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to the colleagues from the Prosecution. I am Vasvija Vidovic, and together with Mr. John Jones I appear for Mr. Naser Oric. We are joined this morning by our legal assistants, Ms. Adisa Mehic and Ms. Jasmina Cosic, and our case manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Vidovic, and good morning to you. Any preliminaries?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's bring the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's bring the witness in. And how much time do you think you will take with this witness so that we prepare the other documents for the other witness because I left them in my room.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do think I'll take the first period and part of the second period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what I imagined, yeah. Thank you. I just asked you in case we need them during the first period then I would have to have them brought over, but it's already more than enough documents on my desk here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Malagic, and welcome back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Hopefully this will be your last day in this courtroom, and then you can go back home. We are continuing with the cross-examination. May I just remind you that are you still testifying under oath. Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Malagic, how are you?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. Fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Good. Mr. Malagic, you testified on your first day of giving evidence before the Tribunal concerning the attacks in Likari and that Naser Oric and his men from Potocari came to assist the attack that you were present at on July 2nd. You confirm that testimony; right?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And you testified that Mr. Oric was physically ahead of the men behind him. Is that the intent of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was walking in front of those men from Potocari when they used to come to Likari.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And you sincerely testified that those are Naser's men, so I would ask you not only was he physically ahead of them, he was the head -- Naser was ahead of Naser's men. Right?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were fighters in Naser's group from Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Malagic, Naser was the head of Naser's group of fighters. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the leader of the group of fighters from Potocari. That's what I said, and we called them Naser's men or the Potocari men or Naserovci as we used to be called Osman's men or Osman's lads or just the people from Voljavica, what have you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Right. Those nicknames were fairly common among the fighting men, you would agree?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would like to show you now -- thank you. I would like to show you a series of videotapes that concern the fighting in Likari, and I would just ask you to watch your screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, these are transcripts that actually come from Prosecution evidence 329 from an interview. So I would just ask the Trial Chamber to ... I understand we're having trouble with the sound for a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I am not receiving any sound.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Neither am I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is a humming noise, but that's about it. Otherwise, no sound.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, might I suggest until this problem is resolved that I just move on in my questioning?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah. Of course. One moment. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: He will call the technicians, but we have to make sure there is sound.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is sound in this because I've seen it more than twice already, sound in the original language and also in the translation, so it's ...

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, it's not -- let's move on --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly. I'll move on. Today is rather tight.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Malagic, we'll get to those tapes in a minute. I'll move on to a related area of questioning. Yesterday you were able to inform me that because of the radio positioned in Likari that you were able to receive communications from the Bosnian Serbs. And Madam Vidovic asked you several questions about the type of information that you received, and your testimony was that that information included the formation of Serb units, positions of Serb artillery, position of different types of strategic battle plans of the Serbs. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of those conversations of theirs, we would then carry out further analysis. When they discuss something, we would then analyse it and reach certain conclusions. And some things they would say themselves because they had no protection for their communications and they knew that we had no communications systems, and that's why their communications were not encrypted in any way. And they even mentioned the names quite openly in -- just in case you're interested. On one occasion we were listening to General Mladic talking to Paca [phoen] on a given frequency because that radio device had a number of different frequencies. So we were just looking through various frequencies and some messages were encoded but most of them were not protected. And I do remember quite clearly that we were listening to General Mladic talking to Paca, I believe, and I can't tell you exactly what it was about. It was a very brief conversation, but they had no encryption, no protection for their communications in their -- in that particular area.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So, Mr. Malagic, you would agree that you were receiving vital information from the armed enemy on a daily basis or on a very frequent basis. Can you say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a way, yes. For what we were interested in, in as far as Likari was concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: You just testified now that when you received that information you analysed the information. Now, how did you analyse that information? Could you just clarify that testimony for me.

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can. If we heard a new -- a known name -- I mean, for example -- for example, we heard the name of Jovan Nikolic called Jole mentioned in the area of Pobrdje, we knew that he was from Kravica and we knew that together with this unit from Kravica he was involved in the fighting around Likarica [as interpreted]. We would then conclude that they had received reinforcements because we all knew that that person was from Kravica and if he moved to this area we would draw our conclusions. Or, for example, they would say we've got guests from Krajina. And we knew that as soon as those people from Krajina came along we would be subject to fierce attacks. And if they said call the Reds to Sase, and they were in Kunjerac normally, and then we would expect attacks. So we had to do that because of our own interest, very often we were saved by that sort of information because then we could prepare better.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, when you say "we" I imagine that you're speaking about Osman Malagic's men, that you're speaking about men of Nasir Sabanovic, that you're speaking --

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Naser's men. And who are the other persons you're referring to when you say "we needed this information"?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I say "we," I mean the people who were at Likari at that time, the group of Osman Malagic. I was there. Osman was killed on the 12th of July and was then replaced by Zajko Alic and Nasir Sabanovic up until the 2nd of July when he was wounded in an attack by Serb forces. He was there, but then he was seriously wounded and he didn't come back. But his people from Potcaus were there with us. So what I mean is the men that were at Likari all the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Malagic, you would certainly think that this important information should also be available to people, Muslims who were not just at Likari but who might have been in Srebrenica, Potocari, who might have been on other places of the front line. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They would have been interested if it was anything about Suceska, Karacici, Osman, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So you must have been very careful as to how you took this information in, and that's what I want to ask you: Did you ever write the information down or did you just memorise it?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We never described anything and we had nobody in charge listening to this. It was just when we were not in trenches that we found it kind of interesting and we were sitting listening to that radio. And sometimes there was nobody there, but it wasn't a constant duty. We were not forced to follow. It was just of interest for us to listen what names they were mentioning and, for example, if they asked for support by mortar, that was Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. of course of interest because if you are being shelled from two or three different locations and of course you must look for a better hiding place. That was what we were most interested in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just a clarification for the transcript. The witness said "we never wrote anything down." And it said: "We did not describe anything" in the transcript. I think that there is a semantic difference there. Could you please describe this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I said we never wrote anything down.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Apologies from the interpreters; acoustically, we didn't hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: You never wrote anything down, but did you tell anyone outside the group in Likari, meaning Osman Malagic's group and Naser Sabanovic's group, did you keep just among those two groups?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no need to say anything to Sabanovic's group, because they were up there, as I said before, his men from Potcaus. So they would listen to it in the same way as we did. What I mean is the group led by Nasir Sabanovic from Potcaus, I did say that they were together with us at Likari, and --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So, Mr. Malagic, if I understand correctly, this vital information, information that could save lives, to protect property, was a subject of conversation and only that for the men who were positioned at Likari. That's what I'm to understand. Correct?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On one occasion, and I've mentioned this in my statement two days ago, when Pirici was about to be attacked and we knew about that, that was the only time we sent Samir Omerovic to the area of Pirici and Poloznik to inform me head Salihovic about that upcoming attack because they were not aware of it up there, and I said that unfortunately in the course of this fighting that young man was killed. His family was up there, and so he himself asked to be allowed to go and inform them, and unfortunately he got killed up there at Pirici. That was the only time when we actually wanted for that information to be forwarded to others. All the other information could be listened to by people from Gostilj, for example, who were there on occasion. It is a village near Potocari and they were often at Likari and they would spend the day there and go back home in the evenings, and they knew of all that information. So there was no need for us to tell them anything. At that time, everybody cared of them -- about their own interests and about their own people.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: You've mentioned Mido Salihovic. Is -- Midhat Salihovic. Is that person also named by the name -- known by the name as --

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Midhat Salihovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Is he also known as Mido, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Okay. So if I'm understanding you correct, you were able to not transmit any of the information that you learned except for the one unfortunate time with the lad Omerovic because there was another receiving post or station near Potocari and Gostilj. So there were other receiving stations so you didn't have to share information outside of Likari. That's your testimony.

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you misunderstood. What I said was this: Occasionally there would be people from Gostilj at Likari. It is a place not far from Likari. They would spend the day at Likari and go spend the night in their own homes. So they were able to listen to that information at Likari. And in case they were interested, they could make use of such information. If they didn't make use of it, it was up to them really.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So there was a casual exchange of this military information between people in Likari and Gostilj. If they came, they might hear about the formation, the Bratunac unit, or they might hear about Serb positions, or they might hear about weaponry? Yes or no? I don't mean to cut you off. I want to keep your answers short because we have a lot of material to get through today.

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I suppose you would have been interested had you been in the area at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So did Mr. -- well, your leader, Osman Malagic, or Nasir Sabanovic, do you know if they ever went to Srebrenica or ever spoke with other leaders to convey the information that was being received from the radio station in Likari?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that Osman Malagic was killed on the 12th of July. Up until then he would only go to see his mother, take a shower, and certainly he was not attending any meetings.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Okay. Is that also the case for Nasir Sabanovic?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nasir Sabanovic was wounded in an attack on the 2nd of July, very soon after we arrived at Likari, and then he never showed up at Likari ever again. What I mean is that he was never again seen at Likari after the 2nd of July.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did any of the other men who were in your group stationed at Likari to your knowledge go to Srebrenica or to other areas in order to transmit this important information?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did you ever tell civilians this information because it might assist them as they were going to look for food?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on many occasions, especially when we had information about roads being closed or important communication lines being cut off, communication lines that would have been used by these people. When we got information about ambushes or minefields we would always inform the civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So did you inform the civilians in Likari or did you inform a broader range of civilians, those in Potocari, those in Srebrenica, those that might still be in the outlying villages?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All civilians looking for food in this area had to go through Likari or just below Likari. And therefore, we did not go to Srebrenica and tell them from house to house. But when they set out to look for food, we would then tell them: You're likely to get killed, ambushes are being prepared, mines have been laid, don't fool around. And it happened quite often, sometimes if some of them stepped on landmines, we had to go and provide assistance and get them out of there. I did tell you yesterday that I myself was present on one such occasion and a man had to have his leg amputated without any anaesthetic and -- by a device which is not really appropriate and his name was Zajko Alic from Voljavica, and his leg was amputated at Gostilj. And we were there because he asked us to stay and give him some support and encourage him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So, Mr. Malagic, would you station -- or would the people from your group of male fighters, be stationed on the road so they would be able to inform civilians, if any civilians went by, about information come in from the different front lines and in particular about what the Serbs -- the armed Serbs were doing?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've said that before.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, after Osman Malagic was killed you had a subsequent leader. To your knowledge did he --

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did he ever go to Srebrenica or talk with other leaders about this vital information that you were receiving from Likari?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He never attended any meetings. We only went to Srebrenica when we wanted to take a shower or change of clothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. It's just a reference to vital information and it's the second time my learned friend has referred to information, important information. The witness has given evidence about information which was of local interest and one or two examples of information which might be of a broad interest. Without specifying what information Ms. Sellers is talking about, I'm afraid you're going to get misleading evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, certainly. I was trying to accelerate the time. Let's go over what the information was because Mr. Jones thinks it was more of local interest, and let's see if the terminology would be correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones must have seen me looking at him because I had exactly the same objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Malagic, I just want to remind you of some of the testimony you said that concerned what was communicated to you. A question had been asked: "Would you please comment on the contents of a document, and it was concerning the Bjelovac company." And your answer was: "The contents means a lot to us. While listening into their communications we knew about this problem that they had. They were frequently criticised by the garrison command because they were not holding the bridge in Bjelovac as well as this bunker. That was important to them and that was on the road to Kunjerac. Later they captured the bunker that was important to our people who we going toward Bejaci [sic] for the food because it was -- it was controlling this road ..." Sorry. "It was controlling this road along with people -- along which people had to pass."

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Let me also read some other information that was communicated to you. The last information I read was on the transcript at page 76, and this is transcript of the 26th of September. This information is on page 77 of the same transcript. There was a question by Madam Vidovic; it concerned information concerning the Bratunac garrison from a document. And then she concluded her question by saying: "I would like now to ask you also about the communication that you monitored over the radio. In October at this time, in mid-October, did you know of the existence of the Podravanje [sic] Company, the Red Beret platoon, and the Sase detachments?" And you answered: "Yes, we knew about the formations that existed at those locations." "How did you know this?" And you answered: "We knew about that based on our communications and also during our recent activities -- reconnaissance activities, we could see from neighbouring elevations where the mortars were located at Sase, Andrici, and all of these other locations."

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never mentioned the Podravanje platoon. I am unfamiliar with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would imagine that this was your objection, Ms. Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Excuse me?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I was mentioning Pobrdje and not Podravanje.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Pobrdje.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly. Thank you very much. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Your Honour, I could go on with different examples of communication, but I am referring in the main to communications received from the Serb armed forces or, as the witness has characterised, battalions. Now, the characterisation of that should be referred to is local information or --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I'm asking you: Wasn't that information that was important and that was vital to the Muslims in Likari, in the -- on the front lines in Srebrenica, Potocari? Could you answer that?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The information pertaining to the Bjelovac Battalion and Sase were very important to us because those two battalions were directly attacking us and they were within that zone encompassing Likari and they could attack from the direction of Sase, Zalazje, as well as on the other side from Pobrdje, Voljavica, and from the wider area of Bjelovac. Hence, such information was of crucial importance for us and we also knew of some other information that didn't pertain to us directly. We liked the fact that we learned about it, but it didn't pertain to us directly. For example, some units like the one in Podravanje you mentioned, that was relatively distant and we were not directly interested. We were always interested in what was happening in our immediate surroundings. And of course at the locality of Pirici and Poloznik, which is close to Bjelovac. We had thousands of our people there. Some of our fighters had their parents together with other refugees there and there were thousands of people there without protection from shells and the rest. That's what impacted directly on our activities.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I proceed with that type of characterisation on the evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course you can.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Okay. Fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Malagic, in terms of communicating this vital information, you've indicated that it was done orally to people who might have been at Likari, to civilians who were passing. Isn't it possible that this was also done at times on a more formal basis to other leaders of Muslim fighters and armed groups?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If one of the leaders was at Likari, for example, came to our assistance, they would ask if there was anything new. And of course we would share that with them. I don't remember exactly, but perhaps they would come and sit by the radio device to listen to the conversations. I know of that one at Likari. I don't think there was any other radio device, but it was always interesting for everyone if you knew somebody's voice you could sort of think about that person, think about where they might be deployed. And at Likari, certain groups of people did come to our aid and then they would ask us as to whether there was anything new concerning the overall situation, and maybe they would sit next to the device and listen. That was interesting. Why wouldn't they? Everyone would be interested.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Well, are you aware of any courier service that might have existed between places such as Likari, Potocari, Srebrenica, people actually carrying messages or information concerning military or civilian? Are you aware of that? And please keep your answer to yes, you're aware, or no, now you're not aware.

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I know that no such thing existed. I would have known for sure had it been in existence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've been informed that we're able to go to the videos. If you just allow me one second with the case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see that it's running but there is no sound.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: "INTERPRETER: At that moment a courier came to the house where my parents were. I was there with 15 of my fighters, who were there waiting for me. The courier came into the house and told me, he said, Naser, commander, I come from Ramiz and he does -- with a message that the Chetniks are preparing an offensive from the direction of Bratunac towards Potocari. The moment that he said that, firing broke out from infantry weapons. I didn't know what was happening, but we all immediately -- each man took his own weapon, and we ran from Gornji Potocari towards Donja Potocari. And then from Donja Potocari you need to climb up to the point of Likari, because this -- this point was the most important to us."

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Malagic, after watching this video, do you understand that there might have been couriers that you had no knowledge of that were transmitting information?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard very distinctly everything Mr. Oric said. He said: Ramiz sent me, Ramiz sent the courier. Ramiz at that time was not at Likari. Ramiz could have sent a courier from Srebrenica to warn him of the attack, so that needs to be clarified. Ramiz -- there was no Ramiz at Likari and no courier was sent. If you have Ramiz Becirevic in mind, he was in Srebrenica. He may have sent a courier from Srebrenica because they heard some shooting at Likari. But from Likari, never a single courier left. I understood well, I guess, that he said Ramiz sent a courier.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Malagic, you did understand well and that's exactly what I'm saying, that there were courier systems. I'm not saying one came from Likari; I'm saying that there were couriers -- courier systems to transmit information at that time just as you have understood. So I believe that we are both understanding the video in the same way. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Don't ask me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Wait one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My learned friend is now referring to courier systems. We've had reference to a single courier and so certainly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: -- on the basis --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]. I apologise to you. Yes, I agree with you, although there is a question earlier on which indicated or hinted to the witness that there was a sort of a system in place, one or more couriers, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, but he didn't accept it and in the video --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- accept it, so I would restrict it to this particular instance that he's told us about, that he's acknowledged.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Can I just check and see whether he's answered the question?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Malagic, I did ask you, as a matter of fact, that what you are saying is that courier to transmit information from that time did exist as you've understood it --

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I just wanted to rephrase what you had said earlier. So do you, by looking at this video, accept that a courier from Ramiz Becirevic did contact Mr. Oric concerning the events at Likari? Can -- did you understand that from this video?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said that at Likari there was any courier, at least where I was at Likari.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And I never -- I don't believe the video says that either. But you agree that the video said that there was a courier that came to Mr. Oric. It didn't say it came from Likari.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's -- because I want to make sure that the witness is not confused. Your question was clear, not this previous question. However, I think that it may have not been understood well by -- by the witness. Because while you were asking the witness to confirm that this is what is stated in the video, he answered -- or then you asked him: "I just wanted to rephrase what you said earlier. So do you, by looking at this video, accept that a courier from Ramiz Becirevic did contact." I mean, that's different. Because your question precise to -- was not whether he accepts, because to accept it, it means that he knew it personally, that --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I prefer the original question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. So I would rephrase it. I think he's followed the exchange now between us, and he can then answer --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, could you please just restate that question? We don't have the questions that go back up that far, and that's purely what I want Mr. Malagic to answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The question that was put to you and which you were asked to agree with was put to you that: What is stated in the video recording is that a courier was sent from Ramiz Becirevic to Naser Oric. Do you accept that that is what is stated in the video?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, on the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then from the factual point of view, I mean I'm not getting involved in that myself. If you want to get involved, please do, but ...

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Malagic, my next question is: Do you know whether there were any courier systems operating in Potocari or Srebrenica or in the area during this time period when you were gathering information?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was no system that was worked out to link up those groups to transfer information. For example, in this situation that we may have sent a courier to Ramiz and Ramiz to Naser, that was not so for sure. Perhaps Ramiz heard shooting at Likari and then sent someone to Naser at Potocari to tell them to go and assist those people there. That is a possibility, but it's not a worked out system of couriers in that sense.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Malagic. Now, I want to refer you back also to your testimony because on the 27th of September, day two, Madam Vidovic asked you: "Could you tell us whether" -- and I'm reading from page 6 of that transcript. "Could you tell us whether you had any information from the scouts from Piricko Brdo regarding the area that they were able to see?" And, Mr. Malagic, you answered: "Yes, they frequently reported back to us. Midhat Salihovic would report back to us that they couldn't stand the pressure there anymore from the artillery, from the direction of Bjelovac, Kunjerac, Sikirici, and that it was terrible." Now, I would like to ask you, this frequent reporting back from scouts, how did you receive that information, in what manner?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We come from the same area, Voljavica and Biljaca are perhaps 2 to 3 kilometres away. There was a lot of our people in Pirici, and those people were moving about. If they couldn't use Biljaca to -- as a route, then they went through Likari. So they moved daily. Sometimes we saw Midhat Salihovic in Srebrenica when we went to take a shower and he would come into town to see his parents. And then we would talk about the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. events at Pirici and we would tell him what was happening at Likari and we would also learn as to whether someone was killed or not. People were moving about daily in their search of food. You could see columns of people. It was a long way, but people did go by foot. We never received any reports but we simply received information. People would tell us because they moved about, they communicated. On occasion one of our people would go up to Pirici to see his parents who were there with the other refugees. And then up there they would learn something new.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. You answered Madam Vidovic's question because she asked you specifically: "Did you have any information from the scouts?" Could you tell us, who were the scouts? Because you said: "They frequently reported back to us." And you gave as an example Midhat Salihovic, Mido, would report back to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment before he answers. Ms. Vidovic, going back to that page from the transcript to which Ms. Sellers referred to earlier, we heard the word "scout," "scouts" there. When you were putting the questions to your witness, what word did you use in your own language?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't remember having used a word "scout." I may have said "an observer." I never used the word "scout" but we can go back to the video recording. An observer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... so much experience here. This is what I suspect, that --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] An observer, somebody who observed it, in that sense of the word. Or someone who was a part of reconnaissance, but I can't be sure at this moment. We will check --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I may offer some clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Malagic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I also found myself in that role, too. You go to an elevation point and you observe. You can call that person a scout, an observer, whatever. For example, Zajko would send two or three of us to see what was happening. So I guess this is just a play of words. I don't think it's so important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you've missed the point that I wanted to make. I wanted to make sure that the word "scouts" now is being interpreted to the witness with the same word that Ms. Vidovic used when it was translated as "scouts" to us. This is what I want to make sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because if the word "scouts" appeared in the transcripts in relation to -- to a descriptive word that she used I want to make sure the same word is being used now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know because I was following the transcript in English, of course, not in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So was I.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Malagic, at times you played the role of the observer/scout. Sometimes you're a commander. Zajko would send you and several others to observe and bring back that information. That's what you've just testified to. How often did you play that role?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Commander Zajko is a somewhat comprehensive term. In order to be a commander you needed to have a unit or people to command over.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I understand that. We're going to get to this terminology. Could you answer my question: How many times did you play the role? How many times did Commander Zajko send you out to be the observer, you and several other people -- a few other people you had mentioned?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The leader, Zajko, perhaps sent me once a week, not that often.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And would he also send other people from your group out to observe other than you?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And did people from other groups such as Miro Salihovic observe and exchange information with you and your groups?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In their part of Pirici and Poloznik, they observed from there. And I told you how we went about exchanging information. We used the people who were moving about.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to go to your testimony, it is again from day two. On page 14 when you were asked the question: "As regards this tank, did you mention artillery weapon in Bjelovac and Sase?" Now, within that answer, you answered "yes" --

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And within that answer, it's a lengthy answer, I want to go midway down, you state: "And it was facing Likari in the Sase area and on Tablja," there is a word missing after that. "And our men in Pirici told us that they had seen a Howitzer in Jovanovici." Now, how did "our men" in Pirici inform you of this?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained already. We used the people, the civilians, when they went searching for food. That's how we communicated. Or when we ran into someone in Srebrenica, when we went there to take a shower, and then we would exchange the information we had. There was no other type of system. We didn't have any radio devices, we didn't have the courier service that would link various areas. That was too risky and too distant. So the only way was to meet -- meet anyone and discuss information with them. You mentioned the Howitzer turned towards Tablja. I said from the direction of Tablja towards -- you said towards Sase, but not towards -- but from Sase towards Likari. So I guess it was misinterpreted.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So I'm to conclude that this exchange of information concerning Howitzers was really done on a fairly casual basis, civilians that would go by or people that you might meet in town as opposed to any type of regulated or structured basis. That would be your testimony, right, Mr. Malagic?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was an informal way but the people that were killed by such artillery pieces died very literally and formally so.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. I'm going to move to just a slightly different area, and that is back to the original videos that I wanted to show. And it will be a series of three short videos that I would ask you to look at your screen and hopefully we have sound and then just ask you a couple questions concerning them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: "INTERPRETER: So after -- after the shelling and the shooting started and people began to withdraw up into the mountains and into the nearby hamlets. These were underneath positions that the Serbs from Gniona were holding high on the mountain. Seeing the situation, that they were encircling us and that they would capture us all alive, we decided to attack Likari so that -- to drive the Chetniks away from there, so that people would be able to return to their houses and return to where they'd been."

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: "INTERPRETER: The only reason was that -- the main reason was that because of this -- the fighting -- the military action that was going on, they were always dead and got killed -- dead and captured on both sides. Just to give you an example, I just made some notice now when I was coming into the building. I forgot to say when I was talking about the battle, when we took Likari and Zalazje the first time, I had -- I had five of my soldiers -- five of my fighters were killed during that attack. They were captured by the Chetniks and then immediately killed."

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: "INTERPRETER: Everybody was shooting. I don't know where they were shooting or what they were shooting at, but basically we all just went together up into the trench. The moment when Sead jumped into the trench, he shot at a Chetnik and the Chetnik shot at him, and they were both killed at that place. So the Chetnik trenches were not all connected with communication trenches, so they were isolated -- isolated points. Probably they didn't have the intention of staying there for very long, so these were just temporary. And then we all jumped in and then people set off in the two directions, some towards Caus and some towards Likari. We were shouting all kinds of things: Alahu-Akhbar, just to frighten the Chetniks because we knew they were afraid of the Mujahedin. And we succeeded in taking Caus, Pous, Likari, and about halfway through Zalazje. We captured lots of weaponry, including an -- including an M-53."

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Malagic, you just heard Naser Oric talk about some of the fighting that went on in Likari. Now, is that consistent with what you witnessed and saw when you were fighting in Likari and with what you had heard about in terms of the fighting in Likari before you came?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This conversation that Naser Oric was involved in as far, as I can tell, referred to the liberation of Likari. And we were still at Poloznik when they were liberating Likari, so I'm unable to tell you anything whatsoever about this particular fighting because I wasn't there. I don't know what went on as they were trying to free Likari. We got to Likari when it had already been liberated. This was in the beginning of the war when Serbs had torched Likari and I think they held three women captive up there. And then in order to avoid a siege of Potocari, they freed Likari, but I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: But is this consistent with what you've heard about what happened in Likari before you came?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to tell you. We knew nothing about that fighting. We knew that this weapon, 53-calibre weapon that the Serbs had in their trenches had been captured, but we didn't know any other details as to how, in what way, who exactly was killed, or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: You had heard that Naser Oric had fought in Likari on several occasions prior to you coming to Likari?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've -- quite frankly I didn't have that information either. We knew that Likari had been freed but who exactly participated with what group and who exactly was killed, we knew nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: You didn't know that Naser Oric had fought in Likari before you came?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would like to show the witness now Prosecution Exhibit P100.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I see the answer wasn't recorded. He said "no, absolute no."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you for pointing that out, Mr. Jones. Yes, for the record, I heard the witness pronounce those words, too. So his answer was"no."

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: It's in Sanctions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Malagic, I would just ask you to read over this document. As you can see it's a document that comes from the Srebrenica TO, Territorial Defence, Crisis Staff. The date is the 3rd of July, 1992. It was stamped by the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Ministry of Defence, BH army, confidential. The date was the 3rd of July, 1992. It's a report of Srebrenica to the staff. And the first paragraph says: "The most violent attacks so far against positions held by the forces of the Srebrenica TO took place in the early morning hours on the 2nd of July, 1992, by the SDS extremists and forces from Serbia on features Caus, Likari, and Zanik." Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honours, just for the record I had been informed prior to coming into court today that the word "koca" [phoen] has been translated as "features" and that a better translation would be "elevations." So where the word features appears, that elevations --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The thing is I'm looking at the document on Sanction here and I want to make sure that this is the document that you are reading from because I can't -- I can't find in it what you read.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm checking that with our case manager. There are two documents that are similar. May I ask with the assistance of the usher to place this on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it will be more practical. This is different, definitely. It's not the same document we had before.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Might I ask that it just be positioned a bit so that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Usher, please, if you could move it further down so that we can -- or further up. Yes, that's perfect. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Malagic, my question to you is that you were present on July 2nd at the fighting in Likari. That's been your testimony. And would you agree with this document that there was violent -- the most violent attack so far against positions included those on the elevations of Likari?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a powerful attack on Likari on that day as far as I know, but I would tend to disagree with this document for a number of reasons, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Could you remove the document from the witness now. Oh, I'm --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Malagic, I will be able to get back to you later. I just wanted to ask you that one question and to move along, and then you'll be able, if necessary, to give any commentary. Okay?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would now like to show Mr. Malagic Prosecution Exhibit 116. Your Honour, I was told this was in Sanctions but we're just having a -- here it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can see it now, but I -- of course, I don't see the document number. The document that I am seeing is dated 14th July, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Your Honour. It's the same document. This is a document, as Your Honour has stated dated the 14th of July, Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Municipal Staff of the Srebrenica armed forces, and it's to the Main Staff of the BH armed forces in Sarajevo and to the district staff of the BH armed forces in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Malagic, if you read through this document it says on the third paragraph down -- no, the fourth paragraph, excuse me. "It is very important to mention that in addition to casualties on the aggressor's side they also suffered material losses, two armoured personnel carriers and an M-84 tank were destroyed. Another tank was completely disabled with a direct hit from our artillery. "A three-barrel PAT was also destroyed. A large quantity of ammunition was seized next to it and a large quantity of infantry weapons was seized: 276 pieces and a significant quantity of ammunition. Four PAMs, anti-aircraft machine-guns, and about 3.000 rounds of ammunition for it were also seized. In addition, seven heavy machine-guns and a large quantity of ammunition were also seized." Now, on your plateau in Likari, did you receive information about this? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can see there is a reference to the Zalazje elevation about a kilometre away from Likari. We would have to see and hear it. I apologise. This is addressed to the Chief of Staff of the armed forces in Sarajevo and in Tuzla and apparently this is coming from Srebrenica. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. And I would just draw your attention to -- it talks about several operations --

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would just like to know by what route this might have been delivered to Sarajevo or Tuzla. How could this be possible? After demilitarisation the international organisations were present in Srebrenica. They know that not even a pigeon could have done it, and I really would like to know in what way this document would have reached Tuzla. This is a reference to these quantities of artillery and arms, and in a previous document that you showed me there was this reference to the fact that on the 2nd of July the Territorial Defence was attacked at Likari. And there was Osman Malagic's and another group there. There was no Territorial Defence from Srebrenica at Likari; there were just these two groups.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Malagic, irrespective of the manner in which the document reached the sender, my question to you was: Were you aware of these events?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: We can remove the document from the witness. I would now like to ask the witness to have P90, please. And on P90 we're going to be looking at the English, page 84, and page 147 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Malagic, I just want to bring your attention to a small portion of this document. If you see a paragraph that begins: "Another arm of the resistance in the Bratunac municipality." If you have found that location then we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it is page 147 in the Bosniak version, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to read into the record just a portion of that paragraph. It says: "Another arm of the resistance in the Bratunac municipality was established in the village of Poloznik, independently of the resistance in Konjevic Polje. The Bratunac municipality fell on 17 April but two volunteer groups refusing to surrender their arms formed two platoons: One in Voljavica led by Osman Malagic and the other in Biljaca led by Sadik Zukic." Now, my question to you is that you have testified that Osman Malagic was your leader and he came from Voljavica. Correct? And you've also testified that the group led by Osman Malagic joined up with the group of Sadik Zukic when you went to Poloznik. Correct?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not what I said. I said that when we were driven out of Voljavica we met with a group of people from Biljaca in Poloznik and they went to a hill called Piricko Brdo and we stayed in Poloznik. And here it says we didn't relinquish the arms. You should ask the Serbs. They are going to tell you and they certainly have the documents to support it, that in Voljavica the arms had been relinquished. What it says here, "the group of young men who did not relinquish their arms." But there is a reference in the documents. I myself relinquished my own rifle and I got it and a reserve officer, and they certainly have this data. So this is incorrect. And that we met in Voljavica, I said that when our people were driven out from those villages, Poloznik and Pirici, we gathered up there to protect those people. I don't know who drafted this document. Somebody who probably wanted to boast a little bit, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: You don't know who the author of this is?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Okay. Is it correct that Osman Malagic was one of the leaders and that Sadik Zukic was one of the leaders, that you came from Voljavica, that the other group came from Biljaca, and that you joined together?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: You can remove the document from the witness. Your Honour, just very briefly before the next break I would like to ask the witness one or two questions and show another video, and I think that will just take us up to 10.30.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Malagic, now you're a professional soldier. You're a member of the army.

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And as a member -- yes. As a member of the army, you are quite familiar with proper army terminology in terms of platoons, battalions, companies, brigades.

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And I would like to ask you that it might seem rather inaccurate if not bizarre to be referring to configurations or groups of fighting men as platoons, brigades, units, that are not technically that under current military terminology. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that stage, it wasn't possible to have any military formations.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Excuse me. My question was: Would you agree that it does seem maybe inaccurate or bizarre to refer to groups used in that --

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would like to ask you whether it might seem inaccurate, if not bizarre, to be referring to configurations or groups of fighting men as platoons, brigades, units, that were not technically that, those terms, under what would be current military terminology. Wouldn't you agree that it would seem inaccurate, if not bizarre?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You mean in the circumstances prevailing at the time?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm trying to see whether from his current military formation that he would think that referring to them with the inaccuracies are, and then I was going to ask him about in terms of 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Go ahead. Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm not surprised if the witness has difficulty with that question there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm not surprised either.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Because on the one hand it's something which is tautological. It's obviously inaccurate. It describes something in terms which it's not. That's obviously inaccurate. So obviously the -- my learned friend is going to get a yes to that answer. But then she keeps inserting "if not bizarre," so then the witness is going to seem to be accepting that something is bizarre which entails a whole other set of circumstances. So if she could ask a simple question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you ought to put the second question that you had in mind of putting first and then you ask the first question after. And I think it will be much easier for him to answer it at that point.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Malagic, did it seem inaccurate in 1992 to be referring to the configuration or group of fighters as platoons, brigades, battalions, to you?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such military formations were not mentioned at the time. Those groups were defined according to their leaders' names or the places where they came from. People from Potocari, from Suceska, Naser's people, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Osman's people, within the framework of the existing villages, that's how they got their names. There were no military formations. I suppose you must be familiar with military terminology. You know what a company is. You would have to have over a hundred armed men and you would have at least three platoons and commanders and everything. At that time we did not have the necessary preconditions. It might have existed -- it could have existed in the areas of Tuzla, Sarajevo, Zenica, and so forth. But in that particular area there was just no possibility for such a thing and there was no need for it either.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So, Mr. Malagic, would that seem inaccurate to you to refer to those groups or configurations by that military terminology?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's incorrect to talk about companies, battalions, brigades, what have you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: But isn't it also possible -- you allow for the possibility that, even with such inaccuracies, people did refer to groups, units, platoons, commanders, and such military terminology in 1992 during that time period?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up until the demilitarisation of Srebrenica, not a single military formation had ever been mentioned. And I'm talking in terms of military terminology. There were no references to platoons, companies, battalions, brigades, nothing at all. In order to have such military formations, you would have to have a battalion command, logistical support. If someone were a member of such a military formation, they would ask for uniforms, weapons, food. Those were volunteers, little groups formed by volunteers. I could have left Likari at any point. I just could have said, Okay, my parents are starving, I'm off to look for food, and nobody would have stopped me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Malagic, you heard on the videotape that Naser Oric was referred to as "commander," yes or no?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we stop here --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we can take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- And we will run the video after the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will have a 25-minute break starting from now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sellers, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Malagic, this is going to be our last period of questioning and then I'm sure Madam Vidovic and Your Honours will have some questions for you. So I'd like to move effectively, efficiently, thoroughly, but as quickly as possible. Okay. Now, the last question I asked you was: Do you remember on a previous videotape that I showed you this morning that Naser Oric referred to himself, saying that Becir -- Ramiz Becirevic had referred to him as commander. Do you remember that on the videotape? If I can help you remember, you've been questioned whether he should be commander. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Me or Naser?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I can only speak directly to you, sir, to I'm asking you the question. Do you remember that Naser Oric was referred to as commander on that videotape? Let me just say it simply.

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we are talking about the period prior to the demilitarisation, there was no commander. Had I had a commander then, I would have gone to see him and I would have told him, we need boots, we need food. But otherwise we would start eating each other at Likari because in the -- during the Leningrad siege cannibalism happened so I believed that something similar would have happened. And I would have asked from the commander to provide, be it Naser or someone else. Nobody could be commander of all those groups at that time. We were very dispersed and no one could link those groups up.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me show you the next videotape, and that's going to be Prosecution Exhibit P433.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would just like to say that there are transcripts to pass up from the videotape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do they tally with what we were reading --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Underneath the --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, they do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because I always want to make sure that the translations are acceptable to both parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We'll have to check the translation. I heard Boci [phoen] so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's why I'm saying in case you have difficulties or any problems with the translations, please speak out as early as possible so as to avoid questions based on expressions which may not be acceptable to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, I might indicate straight away that we heard Boci, which we always translate as "fighters," translated as "soldiers."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Malagic, on the video that you just saw did you recognise anyone on that video?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recognised the journalist. He is from Glogova, and I know who Ahmo was. Not personally but I knew what he looked like; that's the leader.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Is that Ahmo Tihic?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Ahmo Tihic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And do you agree that on that video that Ahmo Tihic responded to the word "commander"?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I wanted to explain. We have different terminology in each of the video clips. This one runs against the previous one. Here Ahmo Tihic is called commander; therefore, Naser couldn't have been. As far as I know Ahmo was the leader of the Biljeg group and he was called commander here. So each one of your documents runs contrary to the previous one.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And do you also recognise that the word "combatant" -- when referring to Ahmo Tihic's group of men, that he used the word combatant?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's nothing new, a combatant, a fighter defending his village.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And you can see what was there -- what their equipment was like.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. And do you also recognise that one man was asked: "Were you the leader of a platoon?" And he said: "Yes."

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that. I heard him say "yes."

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So would you at least agree that people did use military terminology, although from your point of view the use of that terminology in 1992 might have been inaccurate?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The terminology is absolutely incorrect. They may have split in several groups using such terminology so that Ahmo could reach each of the soldiers. But he delegated some of the responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'd like to remind you that you testified that in terms of the Serb army that it evolved from a TO structure, then to an army structure, that that is how it grew. Do you remember that testimony? And you have to say yes or no to the microphone, sir.

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would now like to show Mr. Malagic a subsequent videotape. If you could just bear with me one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I understand these problems, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is P441.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Malagic, after reviewing this video, do you allow for the possibility that there were commanders of self-organised groups and an overall command of the commanders and the self-organised groups, as Naser Oric said at the second anniversary of the formation of the Srebrenica TO?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will offer a brief explanation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Well, could you please first just answer my question: Do you allow for that possibility? And then certainly if you --

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was no such a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Okay, fine.

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I comment now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This recording was created after the demilitarisation of Srebrenica; isn't that so? At that time the Tuzla command wanted to make known that there were no groups fighting there. They wanted to establish some sort of position with our command in Sarajevo. So after the demilitarisation things had to be put on paper, names of people as well, so that after the war people could exercise some of their rights. That was for that reason, to show that we were not as Indian tribes, to say that this or that group had this or that leader, but to show that there was some sort of unification so that that could be sent to the Tuzla command, otherwise it would look like Tuzla fought for itself. But this was to show that Srebrenica also played its role in the liberation war. So it had to be put on paper, signed, and archived. Had we shown them that at that time we only had group leaders, they would have asked us, What were you doing then? You were illiterate, you were incompetent, you didn't organise the resistance movement, but rather you allowed the Serbs to slaughter you. So after the demilitarisation, that should have been shown to Tuzla and Sarajevo, and that's when the lists were made on the military formations. But until then, there were no military formations commanded by a single person and I explained why and I explained what is needed for a commander to have command over his units.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So, Mr. Malagic, according to you, all of the formations that Mr. Oric is talking about were purely for administrative purposes?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those formations were created after the demilitarisation. Ms. Vidovic showed me some documents where one could read, for example, the Independent Voljavica Battalion, then another document --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Excuse me -- pardon me. Could you answer my question. I understand that. All of this was purely for administrative purposes, yes or no, that's the essence of what I believe you're saying?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to move to what will be my final area of questioning.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So I would like to ask the witness now to turn his attention to some of the testimony that you have given this Trial Chamber concerning your participation in Bjelovac. Now, you testified that you went to Bjelovac after your leader had spoken to the leader, Sesmo, and you volunteered -- Huso says, when you volunteered to go there because he -- Husic Sesmo had assisted your family at one time. Do you agree with that, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Mr. Malagic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment because I -- again, I usually while watching the witness I get some feelers. Do you want us to read to you precisely the part of your testimony that Madam Sellers is referring you to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Yes, Ms. Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if the Prosecutor may clarify as to the name. It was -- we were not able to understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I heard a name, but --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I can clarify, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please. Sesmo, something like this.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: The name is Sesmo Husic, and as a matter of fact I can just read your answer after --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Semso Husic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Semso Husic, right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic had asked you the question concerning Mr. Alic: "Did he when he said you had to do something, did he contact anyone else and was any help promised?" And Mr. Malagic answered -- and I'm reading from the transcript now of the 27th of September, I'm at page 20. And Mr. Malagic answered:" Yes. He said that other people had promised to help us return to our villages because people saw what kind of situation we were in." And the following question was: "Did he mention someone specifically?" And Mr. Malagic said: "Yes. He mentioned that he had met Semso Husic, a leader of the group of fighters in Poloznik. He was a man held in high regard because he had helped us while we were stationed in Poloznik." So --

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And then you testified that Semso asked your commander, Zajko, to send an anti-tank weapon and that since you had had experience or knew how to use anti-armour weapons, you volunteered to go. That's your testimony, right, Mr. Malagic? You have to say "yes" into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but eye say Zajko was a commander. I said a leader. Commander is much more comprehensive. You should know that, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I don't want to misuse your terminology. Okay. Now, you were -- you went to -- you went voluntarily with the accord of your leader to Semso and then when you arrived - and now I'm reading from page 21 of the transcript. "In the morning" -- this is your answer. "In the morning very early on the 14th of December, Semso gave us three armed men as escorts and he sent us to Piricko Brdo area, the hill." Now, you went with Suso Huso -- could you pronounce the name, Susic, Huso. Who is it who accompanied you to Piricko Brdo?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Huso Cvrk, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And there when you arrived at Piricko Brdo, you testified that we, meaning Mr. Cvrk and you and the three armed men, improvised an ambush. Is that correct? You have to speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, to your knowledge, was the ambush in Piricko Brdo or your military actions in Piricko Brdo known -- well-known to members of a larger military command, a larger command structure?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So the only people who knew what you were doing was Semso Husic and your own leader, Mr. Zajko. That would be your testimony; right?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't know as to whether other people knew. I don't know that, if anyone else knew. Whether Zajko or Semso told anyone, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like Mr. Malagic to be shown Prosecution Exhibit 84. I'll indicate the page in one minute, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I'll indicate the page in one second, please. In the English it is page 36. The ERN number in the B/C/S is 03090740.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you are saying them --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: They are double ERNs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- the other way around.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The ERN you have just mentioned is the English one. The corresponding one in B/C/S is 02115090, if I am right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's 509 -- 89, it starts on the previous page. You're right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then it has to be the previous page unless you are referring to the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I am referring to the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then it has to be again page 36. But the witness has to be referred to 02115089, and it's the last paragraph on that page. It should be at least anyway, because I'm not seeing it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
