utterances.text: Might I at this time take advantage of giving the usher the transcripts from the previous exhibit that we had referred to.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Malagic, do you see where it's listed under section Roman numeral II, a paragraph that starts: "It was decided to carry out additional reconnaissance on 9 December 1992"?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it but this handwriting is a bit illegible.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Then I'm going to read out that paragraph to you. If there's any corrections, certainly. It says: "It was decided to carry out additional reconnaissance on 9 December 1992 for the continuation of combat activities. On 10 December 1992 at 1120 hours, a staff meeting will be held at which a final decision will be taken. The number of participating units and soldiers will be increased by attaching the Kragljivoda unit which will reconnoitre the Piricko Brdo-Sikiric area. The Biljeg Battalion will join the Voljavica unit and reconnoitre the ambush at Voljavica. Reconnaissance and preparation for the newly discovered trench will be carried out by the Stari Grad unit."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm going to read this out, if the witness can follow, because this translation is incorrect because the grammar is incorrect and the term "unit" is being used where it does not exist in the original. Can the witness please try to follow what I'm reading, I'm going to read slowly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Also -- yeah, go ahead and I will comment later, if necessary. The procedure should be as follows: As Madam Vidovic reads out from the document, this page from P84, I don't know if you have it available - the interpreters - or not, but could you kindly please translate to us not by reference to the English version that we see on the screen, but just translate to us as if you are interpreting under normal circumstances. All right? Yes, Ms. Vidovic, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "The decision was made in terms of the continuation of military activity to carry out additional reconnaissance in the course of the 9th of December, 1992. On the 10th of December, 1992, at 1120 a staff meeting will be held at which a final decision will be taken. The number of participating units and the number of fighters will be increased." Your Honour, I see the same mistake here. I'm not sure that it is the same tense. It is being increased.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters believe the meaning is the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At any rate, the witness is asked to follow. "The Kragljivoda units will be included and they will reconnoitre" -- Your Honour, I am saying "they are being included" and not "they are going to be included."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "And they will reconnoitre the area Piricko Brdo-Sikiric. The Biljeg Battalion is adjoining the Voljavica men and is reconnoitring in Voljavica. Reconnaissance and preparation," and there is an illegible bit of text, but anyway, afterwards it says, "is carried out by the Stari Grad." Is that sufficient? Your Honour, what I am trying to draw your attention to is that in the B/C/S language there is a huge difference between saying "is being joined" or "is going to join." The implications are completely different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Yes. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Madam Vidovic for the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It hasn't actually solved one of the issues that Madam Vidovic raised, because if I heard her well when she first raised the matter, she also objected to the translation of a certain word into "units." Is that correct or not? Because it has been translated into "units" again. So if you think that it should be translated into something else, please tell us so.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it says "the Voljavica men" and not "the unit from Voljavica," as was translated in the text read out by Mrs. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. All right. So you know now what the position of the Defence is as related to this part of the text. So you please --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- can proceed to put your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Malagic, my question is that you testified that Semso Husic sent you to Piricko Brdo. Now, isn't it true that the ambush that you set up at Piricko Brdo was part of a military planning for the attack at Bjelovac?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I arrived to the Poloznik area on the 13th, late at night. And early in the morning, three young men came along and we set off to the Piricko Brdo area. So some additional information was just unavailable to me or anything else about this activity. May I make an additional comment now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Please be extremely brief because we do have to move on?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please go ahead, but be brief as is suggested to you by Madam Sellers, because there is another witness waiting to start giving evidence and he needs to go back home at the end of tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to be very brief. In this report, in this document, the reference is to from the people of Kragljivoda reconnoitring the people from Piricko Brdo. At the same time -- I mean, it would look almost if I were sent to reconnoitre The Hague. I mean, I don't have the map here but people from Biljeg can't reconnoitre Voljavica because they are simply unfamiliar with the area and the same areas to -- the same refers to Kragljivoda and Piricko Brdo. I mean, you're a very nice and charming lady, but I can't think where you Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. get your documents from. You must have realised that they contradict one another --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop, stop. Yes, I'm sure that's --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm very flattered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- not the first compliment that you have received, but I would suggest that you forget about it and proceed with your questions. Maybe the witness will change his mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Malagic, if I could slightly draw your attention to the preceding page, the section of the document that we were reading out concerned a meeting held on the 8th of December and at the beginning paragraph that both Madam Vidovic and I read out it talked about a decision taken on the 9th of December for reconnaissance of that area. My question to you is: When you arrived in Bjelovac - and now I'm talking about when you were physically there on the 14th and you set up the ambush - did you know that that was part of a larger military planning? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I can move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Ms. Sellers. Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, and it may not be necessary now, given the answer, but it's being suggested one ambush in this document and the ambush in which this witness was involved, and they're one and the same, of course. That's an inference drawn by my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, that's how I'm taking it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's an inference by her; it's not something that's an accepted fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He can answer about that. If he doesn't accept it as the -- one and the same thing, then he's free to say so.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Malagic, now I have to take you to a part of that time period that you've testified was rather hard for you. You mention that Sesmo Husic died during that time period, was killed. Could you please just remind the Trial Chamber where he died, if you know.

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was killed on the 14th of December, in the fighting around Kunjerac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. Do you know whether he was with anyone else in the fighting, any other -- well, let me ask you directly. Do you know whether he was with any of the other fighters from Pirici or from that area?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Okay. I would now ask Mr. Malagic to stay with the same document. I am going over to page 38 in the English version and the B/C/S version, the ERN number is 02115092. I would like to draw your attention to the paragraph that begins with: "The ambush in Voljavica around 100 men in two ambushes," but more in particular it is the line underneath that that says: "Kunjerac, Mido and Semso with 20 men each from one side." Now, the date of this section is the 10th of December. I am asking you, it is your testimony that Sesmo died on the 14th in Kunjerac in battle. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on the 14th and on the 10th I was still at Likari and here it says the 10th.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. Now, to your knowledge I would like to ask you whether Mido and Semso, Mido meaning Midhat Salihovic, were they together during the combat operations, actions, on the 14th of December in Kunjerac, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You should have given me a map and then I would have been able to show you. Kunjerac is a hill over Biljaca and the men from Biljaca had to go back there; they're not from Pirici. Midhat is not from Pirici, he is from Biljaca. In order to get back to Biljaca, they had to engage in fighting around Kunjerac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I just have a couple more questions concerning Bjelovac and I would like to refer to your testimony, sir. Concerning the burning of houses or buildings in Jovanovici, I am now on the transcript the 27th of September, page 33, and you were asked by Madam Vidovic: "Could you please tell the Trial Chamber how these houses were set on fire?" Now, your response was: "Whoever would tell you how they were set on fire would be lying. It could have happened from the shooting of our PAM. Whoever said that they knew exactly how they were set on fire would not be telling the truth." And then you say: "It could have been our PAM, it could have been the Serb artillery shooting from across the Drina, it could have been the bombs dropped from the airplane. So there are three causes for the fire in those houses." Mr. Malagic, would you agree that if a house caught on fire before the airplanes had bombed, it wasn't the airplanes that placed the house on fire?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see any houses on fire before the air raid. And I said quite clearly that our PAM was used in order to shoot at houses from which there was shooting directed at our fighters. Any artillery weapon may well set a house on fire. So that might have happened but it's even more true of air raids.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, but then you would agree that a house that caught on fire before an airplane came was not set on fire by the airplane? That's -- yes or no, you would agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's -- because I can anticipate what Mr. Jones is going to say. Let's make myself -- let me make myself clear.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It wouldn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If air raids haven't started as yet, you cannot even speak of houses being set on fire as a result of air raids. So that is eliminated. As regards causes of fire before air raids, he has already told you that he is not aware that any of the houses were on fire before the air raids started. So that's the position of the witness, as I have understood it until now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Okay, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If -- if you think I am wrong, please tell me so. Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I just wanted to have -- if that's his position, have that placed on the record and then I'll have a series of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's not that it's hypothetical about if X and Y happened what would be the consequence be. But I don't really see how a witness can answer a question like that in any event, because, well, what if there's a small fire and a plane comes and drops a huge bomb and destroys the houses. It's a question of degree, it's a question of facts in each case. I don't want this witness to answer a hypothetical about what would be responsible for damage when he has no idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. Jones. No questions hypothetical that would elicit a hypothetical answer. And let's --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just state that this witness had many hypothetical questions posed to him on direct, and I think in cross-examination we are allowed to use, to a certain degree, if he has knowledge of a hypothetical. And I will make it as brief as possible, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but having heard hypothetical questions and hypothetical answers before does not entitle you to continue along the same lines. I mean, we don't really give much attention to hypothetical questions and hypothetical answers because, out of their own nature, they're inherently of no probative value. If they are hypothetical, they will remain hypothetical unless at the end of the day they end up being corroborated with hard facts. So put the question that you would like to put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Malagic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course, I will not stop you, but I gather that his position as regards the causes of fire in the various houses was as I said -- and if I am not right, please go ahead and try to correct --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Right. Your Honour, it seems that he has various hypothetical positions as to how the fire might have started.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Malagic, you were not physically in the houses in Jovanovici during the attack on Bjelovac on that day, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not one of our soldiers, or rather fighters was in the houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: If someone in or nearby their house in Bjelovac saw a soldier set it on fire, you would allow for the possibility that that is how the house burned down. Correct? Yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must tell you that there was no combat in Bjelovac itself. Could you please give me a map. Jovanovici and Loznicka Rijeka are different places all together. There was no fighting in Bjelovac and not a single house was set on fire there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He said --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He said --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Let me just say Jovanovici.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: If someone were in their house in Jovanovici or near their house and saw a soldier set that house on fire, then you allow for the possibility that that is how the house caught on fire, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Okay. And then I'll come up into one of my final questions in terms of Bjelovac. You've testified that not a single armed Muslim entered Jovanovici, Loznicka Rijeka, and Bjelovac. That's your testimony, right, Mr. Malagic?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't put it that way. I said that they didn't enter Jovanovici and that later on I found out that a smallish group of people from the direction of the river Drina got as far as some houses in Loznicka Rijeka. You must make a distinction between Loznicka Rijeka and Jovanovici. So that smallish group of people which was in combat against those special forces, Mungus and Koke [phoen], and probably the planes were used to target those people and their houses in Loznicka Rijeka that we saw. That what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... saying you need to be fair. I'd like you to just be a bit briefer. So I understand your evidence that the smallish group of people came into combat from Jovanovici. I would like you now to turn to the document in front of you and the ERN number, I am on the English page 37, ERN 02115090. Again, we're at meetings of the Srebrenica OS Staff of 10 December 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's the next page.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And I'm going down under section 1, the third Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. paragraph, where it says: "Nedzad Mis can only take the personnel carrier."

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Do you see where I am, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think he can see where you are because if it's 5090, then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then we have to move. Next page, 37. All right. Page 31 -- sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 5091, it's the fourth paragraph before the end. Fourth paragraph before the end. It starts with Nedzad Mis can only take the personnel carrier. Attack Bjelovac from the Drina - the main attack. Bjelovac can fall only when Loznicka Rijeka falls."

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So other than the conversation, Mr. Malagic, with your cousin, were you aware that the main attack of Bjelovac came from the direction of the Drina river?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The main thrust of the attack - and I could see it better than the rest of them - was from Pirici and Poloznik in the direction of the house at Jovanovici. That's where the most fierce fighting took place, the houses in Jovanovici and from the hill near Pirici and Poloznik. And I said that I later found out that a smaller group of people crossed a small river which is called Loznicka Rijeka and they came from the river Drina and they tried to enter that part of Loznicka Rijeka, not Jovanovici, but Loznicka Rijeka. And only in that area there was actual fighting because nobody actually entered Jovanovici and there was no fighting at all in Bjelovac. You keep referring to Bjelovac; Bjelovac is something else. We saw a video and we just saw a school in Bjelovac, and then it's in the direction of Zaluzje [as interpreted], et cetera. And there was no fighting there at all and no houses were set on fire either through fighting or air raids or anything. I mean, later on they started destroying the Bjelovac houses during the winter offensive, but there was no fighting in Bjelovac at that stage at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Malagic, are you unaware that the main attack into Bjelovac, the larger area - I'm using it as it's stated here - came from the Drina River? Yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Fine. Then I would just like to move to one other point within here. Mr. Malagic, you've testified that Hazim Dzananovic was not a commander, was not a leader to any of the armed men in Voljavica. That was your testimony. Correct?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Is it possible that you were --

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Unaware that at a planning level at an -- at a higher command structure, that Hazim Dzananovic was considered to be the unit commander. Does that possibility exist?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hasim Dzananovic came to Srebrenica from Tuzla together with Muriz Dezdanovic [phoen] in August, and throughout that period he was a fighter at Likari together with us, and later on at Voljavica. So I know him quite well. I do apologise, may I add another point?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would really like you to answer my question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you answer the question and just the question, and leave it at that, it will be much better, Mr. Malagic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Just, were you unaware that at a planning level that was at a higher command structure, let's say, than you that Hazim Dzananovic was considered to be a unit commander? Do you allow for that possibility?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew everything about Hazim and I'm hereby claiming that he was no leader, no commander, nothing of the sort.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Might I draw your attention now to the same document in front of you, and the page number will be for the B/C/S 02115109, and that is on page 30 -- I'm sorry, page 50 of the English version. And you will see under section Roman numeral III it's listed 1, 2, 3, 4, and under number 4, under Roman numeral III it says: "The Voljavica unit is requesting independent battalion status. Not accepted. Hazim is a unit commander. Wait for the end of the attack on Jezero and then form a unit." And under number 5 it says: "The Voljevac people are requesting food. Sugar and beans are to be approved." Are you just unaware that that happened? Just yes or no to my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Several times my learned friend asked --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: -- asked whether the witness is unaware of the fact, as if these are all a whole bunch of facts that are contained in this document. It's whether that possibility -- these are merely allegations in a document like this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: But there it's a plain suggestion that here's a fact and he can only be unaware of it if he doesn't know of it. It's whether --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But whether -- I think we have already explained this in the past, that the fact that something is written in a document only means that it is written in a document. Whether it's really happened or not depends on other circumstances, so -- and I think the witness is an intelligent person that he knows exactly. If he's not aware of anything like this having happened, he will tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's simply -- I don't want to put it as a fact, and if he's unaware of it, it's that he's ignorant as opposed to that maybe the fact doesn't exist.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There's always that possibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly, and I don't think that the Prosecution is trying in any form to mislead the witness. I think -- we're on cross-examination, and these are very similar --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But point taken, and you can proceed. I think it's --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So if we would just recap our last question in this area: Are you aware -- excuse me. Are you aware that -- do you allow for the possibility that this occurred, the naming of Hazim Dzananovic, at a higher command structure?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. Now, I would just like to move into my last area. Yesterday, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we had two last areas because the previous one was also --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Subsections, Your Honour. This is the true last area. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Malagic, yesterday you testified that you weren't aware of a military police being in Srebrenica during 1992. I would just ask --

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would just like you to see this very short videoclip, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: "DP: There's no question that those are big problems. Is the military police a branch of the military under which -- of which you were a commander? "NO: Yes."

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So, Mr. Malagic, would it be your testimony that you didn't know that Naser Oric was a commander of the military police during 1992, during that time period? Yes or no please.

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Sellers. Is there re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, Ms. Vidovic. You may remain seated.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Malagic, yesterday during your testimony you were shown an excerpt from a book by Mr. Ibisevic, Besim. It's page 118 beginning with: "Naser Oric, policeman." That was P564.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we could give this to the witness again.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to draw your attention --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that's page 7 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to draw your attention the last part on page 118.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that's just below the middle of the page, number 7.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please take a look at that part. And I will quote the first sentence. "Naser Oric, policeman of the Srebrenica police station," and so on and so forth. I wanted to quote the following, the last part of page 118. "Secret distribution of weapons began. At what price the weapons were bought, most of the members of the staff never learned. Those who had the monopoly over purchasing and distributing of the weapons kept silent. After some rumours, stories began going around but there was no time to verify." Would you agree that the author himself mentioned whispering rumours and stories and that there was no time to verify that?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and he mentioned the people from the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you agree that this is based on unconfirmed stories, as is put here?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now put P72 before the witness. This is a contract that we saw yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Malagic, before the document reaches you I wanted to ask you the following: Did you ever see a sales contract in Bosnia-Herzegovina in your life?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, when I was purchasing some land.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at the document. You can leaf through and look at each of the pages. Are those pages signed or initialled, with the exception of page number 3, or has only page number 3 been signed?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just page number 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said you saw a contract of this nature previously. Would you agree with me that each -- such a contract or an agreement has to have all the pages initialled in our country?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at the date on the document. It states here "the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Srebrenica TO, the 10th of April, 1992." During your testimony you several times mentioned that Srebrenica was freed or liberated. If you can remember, on the 10th of April, 1992, was there any sort of conflict in Srebrenica? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that came about later.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In your knowledge, on the 10th of April, 1992, was there such a thing as Territorial Defence headed by any Muslim person in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At that time people still resided in Srebrenica. Certain groups did flee Srebrenica, those people who felt unsafe to stay together with their families.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would draw your attention to a particular item of this contract, that is item 9. The buyer, being someone represented by Naser Oric, the buyer provides guarantee to the seller that the agreed value of goods will be paid the following way. Argentija auxiliary facility with all of its facilities, Gruber spa with all of its facilities, the forest complex of 500 metres to the right and left of the road, as well as the square up to the area of Argentija up to the last building close to the source." Mr. Malagic, the property stipulated here, was that in public hands in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Gruber Spa goes back to Roman times.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could anyone have provided such guarantees a private person or an enterprise without a separate procedure.

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not even the president of the state could make such an offer.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please go down further on the document. It ends with item 11. Do you agree with me, on page 2. On the Bosnian version page 02075806 it states here item or Article 11: In case of dispute, the court of arbitration will make its ruling. If you now go to the next page, what do you see there, what article?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Article 13.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that Article 12 is missing?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe the -- such a contract should also be verified by a notary public, but it is not such a clarification.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Attorneys could explain that better.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you were asked questions as to whether you were visiting your family in Srebrenica. I followed your testimony closely. Was your family in Srebrenica or in Zabonja, which is a village just outside of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a village outside of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please give P458 to the witness. P458.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please take a look at the first page of the document. Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean page 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The Prosecutor showed something to you yesterday. She claimed that they call this the military police diary, and I can tell you that we call this the Livoda [phoen] diary. But I wanted to ask you the following in relation to that. Is there anything in the title that could indicate that this is a military police log or diary? Is there such a title here?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can see, this is a log in which my uncle is mentioned as being taken into custody by the military police, but I don't think any military police would deal such things.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: We will come to your uncle later. Yesterday the Prosecutor asked you about several names from Voljavica. She read their personal data, for example, date of birth. Do you always -- did you know the answer to all of her questions as to their years of birth?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew some of them for some of my relatives, but I didn't for others.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please now go to page 03593145.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that's page 16 in English, in English version. In Bosnian, that's page 22.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see that?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It says here: Mehmed Malagic, son of Rama, born 1937 in Voljavica, owns an apartment in Srebrenica. I went together with the Jahici men to Voljavica two months ago, and so on and so forth. It says here: "The corn is mine." I wanted to ask you the following: Did you know that your uncle was taken into police custody because of some criminal offence?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The fact that a person from Srebrenica at that time went to look for food, if you found that in any given document that is in existence, would you be surprised by that?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I'm even more surprised because this is apparently mentioned in a military police log. You can see when my uncle was born, so he isn't a member of any group and it is not logical that the military police dealt with that. And I noticed another thing, and you did as well probably: The entire log is in the same handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I wanted to ask you something else. It is mentioned here that he went with two Jahici men. Just go to two pages before that, that is page 0359 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter apologies, we missed the number.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe you could be able to find that. It is a page dated the 14th of December. There is a mention of two Jahic men, Rifat and Ismet.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at the names?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I would kindly ask the usher to put a Defence exhibit before the witness, and then I will go back to this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, this is an excerpt from a census between the 1st and the 15th of April of 1992. This pertains to the local commune of Bjelovac in Bratunac, and you will see here the list of all of the Jahici people in that local commune.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I've also provided a letter explaining how I obtained this material, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at the name in the first column on the last page -- actually the second name, Jahic, Ismet, son of Daut. Do you know this person?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not by his name, but I knew all the people there so I must have known him as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Irrespective that can you take a look at his date of birth. It says Ismet Jahic, son of Daut, born 1938. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my document --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Which column are you looking at? Could you please take a look at this list of inhabitants?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When we saw Jahic, Ismet, in the other document, which is one of the people that allegedly your uncle went there, what is the year there?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And that's also Ismet Jahic, son of Daut?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you agree with me that there were no such people of the same name and with the same father's name there?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I am now going to go back to the latest videoclip. You were shown a very short videoclip, and one gains an impression -- or rather, a question was posed to Naser Oric as to whether he was a commander. And from his answer one is to conclude that he confirmed that. Did you hear what he was talking about at all? Did you hear anything pertaining to the time period that Oric referred to?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted to ask that question from the Prosecutor, but I wasn't allowed to. I wanted to ask her whether that was prior or after the demilitarisation. So the time period is not mentioned at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So you agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the counsel and the witness please pause between question and answer, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, you're moving too fast.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, before we move on, when I was talking about the question put to Naser as to whether he was a commander, I said "commander of military police," and that is not reflected in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, did you understand me in that way, that Naser was referred to as a military police commander?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understood it the same way.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you find page 39?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, if we are talking about the same police log.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: 39 in Bosnian. The date is the 29th of December, 1992.

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The date is the 29th of December, 1992. You mentioned Muhamed Cvrk, do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I will go back to that topic, but before that we will read out the paragraph below. The same person was taken into the military police station based on orders of the War Presidency because he appropriated some equipment, some cutting equipment." Reading this document, what would be your conclusion who issued orders to the military police?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the War Presidency according to this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I wanted to ask you the following: Yesterday you mentioned Muhamed Cvrk. You said you were wounded and that he was wounded. On the 29th of December, 1992, was Muhamed Cvrk in Srebrenica at all, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. To reiterate I was with him and he was in our group with Zajko Alic. He was in Voljavica at that time. Two years before the New Year's Eve. I was wounded, Muhamed Cvrk was wounded, Muhic Mevludin, and Mirsad as well, so four of us, and that was from a hand-grenade.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will no longer need the log. Could the usher now put P100 before the witness. Your Honour, could we assign an exhibit number to this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It wasn't -- I see. I was under the impression that it had already been tendered. This will become Defence Exhibit D77 --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D776, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: D776. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember this document?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps to clarify, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. this is a voluminous document but we did use some portions of it, although not this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: As part of P100, there are several documents. We are interested in that one of the 3rd of July of 1992. You said there were several reasons as to why you thought something was wrong with the document, and you were then interrupted by the Prosecutor. In the second line it says here: "Executed by SDS extremists and some forces from Serbia." On the 2nd of July, 1992, you were at Likari. Who attacked you on that day, the local population or some forces from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were attacked from the direction of Pobrdje and Tablja. So a Pobrdje unit as well as a unit from Zalazje, that is from Sase and that area there.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Does this document reflect the situation in the field?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in any way. And I don't know why somebody had to write such a report. If anyone was to write a report, it was supposed to be us. Osman Malagic was still alive at Likari, and he would have written it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have no knowledge of the existence of such reports?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We never put together such reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any other particular reason to doubt the authenticity of this document?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How come it was directed or sent to the Republican Staff at Sarajevo or Tuzla? It was impossible to reach hem.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You wouldn't now how it came there?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not even a pigeon could get through at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please take a look at P516 again -- P116.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And after this we have a break.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, apart from this one I have just one other question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But we will probably have questions ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we might take the break actually now and then you can finish. One thing because I need an urgent -- a quick reply from you. There is a possibility of moving the sittings of the 4th October, of the 13th October, and of the 14th October from the afternoon to the morning. The three of us are in agreement, but I want to make sure that you are, too. And the 5th is already moved to the morning, the 5th October. All right with the Defence. With the Prosecution it should be less of a problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No problem, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So you can advise the registrar that 5th is already confirmed. We move 4th, 13th, and 14th. Okay? Thank you. We reconvene in 25 minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm just going to ask one question, and it will be with reference to both documents. I'd like to ask the usher to give this document to the witness. Again, I was expecting to see it still there before the witness. I have a question in relation to P00 and P16.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you take a look at the same document you looked at earlier on dated the 3rd of July, 1992? P100. This is a short document --

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do apology, there are two dated the 3rd of July.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Can you look at that document and if you can take a look at the third paragraph which ends in: "The artillery position of TO Srebrenica, so the artillery support from the most modern weapons such as tanks, M-84s; grenades, 102-millimetres; guided rockets; and we have exactly 564 shells fired in the direction of Pale. The artillery position of the TO Srebrenica and the town of Srebrenica itself." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any knowledge in July 1992 of the TO Srebrenica or the town of Srebrenica or whatever of having an artillery position at all? Does this correspond to the facts on the ground?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you now take a look at the other document I submitted to you, P116, P116. It is dated the 14th of July, 1992. And the third paragraph again says: "It is very important to stress that apart from losses incurred by the aggressor in terms of human resources, we also destroyed two armoured transporters, tanks, et cetera, and the second tank is -- has taken a direct hit by our artillery." I would like to repeat the same question: Did we have any artillery and is this weapon, M-84, a tank?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, M-84 could refer to a machine-gun as well, but here it says a tank. It is extremely difficult to destroy such a tank as far as I am familiar with the weapons of the former JNA and we did not have such weapons that could have destroyed them at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Vidovic. Judge Brydensholt. Usher, if perhaps you can leave a message to have the next witness prepared. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: I understand that you had a radio receiver in -- or equipment in Likari. Would -- and in the beginning you had a battery which you used to operate it. If you had had a new battery or further battery, would it have been possible then to move this radio equipment when you went otherwise other places than Likari, to take it with you?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had we had that kind of equipment, we would have been able to do so, but since we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Okay. But else it would be movable?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It could have been fueled in other places. I explained how it was done later on in Srebrenica with many powerplants, as it were. But a good electrician could have done that but it stayed at Likari throughout.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Judge Eser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: First I have a question with regard to terminology. Mr. Malagic, you always rejected the terminology of "commander." You told us that something like a commander did not exist at that time, but instead you would speak of a leader. Now, what did it mean to be a leader of a group?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It meant that such a leader would be surrounded by a smallish group. Had that person been a commander according to military terminology, there would have had to be a battalion or something of a higher order, as far as I can tell, according to military terminology. In this case it was the leader, just one person leading that one group and being responsible for that group and a person that we listened to, basically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: And who would select, appoint, or find out who should be a leader? Was it self-announced that somebody would say, I would like -- I am prepared to be the leader? Or was it some sort of an election by the group of people fighting together?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People amongst themselves would normally appoint, as it were, the person they felt was the most capable to lead the group, somebody who had a higher education than others or was singled out because of courage or something. That's how we viewed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: And now you mentioned that it would have been possible for you, for instance, just to go away if you want to go home to assist your parents for -- rescue them from starving. Now, in these terms of voluntary to join a group or perhaps to dejoin from a group again. But as long as you have been a member of a group, how was it -- let's say there has been a decision to go to Pirici, could you just say, Goodbye? You may do your business, I'm going home. What it meant? Was there a decision? How would it work?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. We lived under such conditions. You could always come up with the reason to be able to say I have to go and look for some kind of accommodation for my parents or whatever; nobody would have stopped you or bound you from doing that because we were all in the same boat. If you had no shoes, you had to go and look for some shoes; if you had nothing to wear, the same. So basically you said it and nobody tried to stop you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Now to get it really clear. Of course I understand that you have been free just to leave, but let's say if your group decided to make a certain type of attack or whatever you may call it and then you went -- started to go to Pirici, for instance, could the members of the group just say, You may go on. I decided not to go along with you all of a sudden. Or have people -- members of the group been expected, if there was a decision taken by the group to go on, that you stay together?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes what? I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Just to stay together.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The translation is still going. I think one has to bear in mind --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, I see. What is your answer to the question?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We never forced anyone to do anything. If, for example, somebody was scared to go and participate in the fighting, he could have said so and not participated. Although normally within our group, if we did go, we went together. And if somebody said they were afraid or was too young, we would try and make it possible for that person not to go. If, for example, somebody's brother had been killed earlier and that person was left alone, we took account of that as well. So it was possible for people not to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, there was another term which appeared in several connections. There was talk about reconnaissance activities. Now, what does it mean to perform these type of activities, reconnaissance activities?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this respect it is about the activities, for example, if we went up to an elevation or something and we'd had a pair of binoculars and we tried to see whether we could see the enemy grouping in any way or whether they were preparing for something or if there was new artillery on their positions. That was essential for us. In that case we could have expected more powerful attacks. So we had to do that, otherwise I wouldn't be here to tell the story today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Now -- okay. Now, as you told us, there have been different points from where you have been able to see movements in the area. Now, how was it done? Could anybody in your group say, I go this way or all given to one point or was it somehow decided member one would go to direction to Pirici, somebody else would go direction to Potocari, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. and so on?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Normally we would do these things in a kind of voluntary way. Those were mountain paths, footpaths. And, for example, the enemy would have arrived at Caus just above Bratunac. There were no fighters from our side and there were no Serbs there. So when we got there, it was still risky and we had to be very careful as to how we could get there. We had to sneak up to those positions on footpaths. And then we would just try and check the situation out very briefly and then go back to Likari where we were stationed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: I think I understand that you talked about the method, the way how you could there. But if there was need to observe different points, has there been a discussion within our group who of you would go this way or who would go the other way? Or was it just the individual decision of one of you to say, I go there and somebody else would go to another spot?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was less essential. We could decide ourselves. Okay, I'll go here or there or wherever. It wasn't so important. We never discussed that at any length at all. If there was something you felt was of interest or suspicious in some way, you could assess the situation even without the knowledge of the leader at any given time. You could just take a walk and check it out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Now, just another point. You have been asked with regard to what Naser Oric may have known or not known. Now, how far away is Likari from Potocari? I think you mentioned 3 to 4 kilometres, something like this.

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It all depends on what route you take. There is the upper Potocari and the lower Potocari, 4 to 5 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you have testified that from Likari you had to go to Pirici and that Mido Salihovic was in Pirici with his group, and that Pirici was never controlled by Serb forces until March 1993 until the demilitarisation, that's on page 11387. Now -- and then you have been asked whether Naser Oric was able to know about this, and you denied it.

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Now, if you will see that Potocari is only about 4 kilometres away from Likari, what makes you so sure that it was impossible for Naser Oric to know anything going on in this area?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said it himself in his own statement that part of Pirici was held by Serbs. So on the basis of that very fact, he didn't know that. But I knew it and everybody else from that area knows that up until March Serbs had never held a single part of Pirici, and I'm certain that Serbs would confirm that as well. More specifically, at that period of time Naser was fighting for Potocari. They had Bljeceva cell in front of them, and there were considerable attacks there and he certainly was not interested in what was taking place at the other end, that is to say Pirici and Poloznik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Now, am I correct in concluding that, when you denied knowledge of Naser Oric to certain events, that you only referred to this event where Mido Salihovic went to Pirici with his group.

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question is not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: My question is the following: You -- from your testimony two days ago one could get the impression that you knew or that you told us that Naser Oric was not aware of things which you may -- you may have known but which he may not have known. Now, in your answer now you were referring to this problem of Serb forces in the area. Now my question is: When you deny that Naser Oric had knowledge of certain events, do you only refer to this event or would you say generally that Naser Oric did not have knowledge of certain things going on in the area?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this case we are talking about Pirici and the Pirici hill held by Midhat Salihovic and his group. So on the basis of his statement, it appears that a part of Pirici, the Pirici hill, was held by Serbs, and it is apparent he was not familiar with the situation in that area. So he did not know. Because had he known, he would have known that there were no Serbs there. It was a Muslim village. They were indeed attacking it all the time from the direction of Sikirici and Jovanovici. But up until March when the winter offensive started, they never actually entered Pirici; they pushed us back in the direction of Srebrenica only at that stage from Voljavica and Biljaca and all these other places. And you know all about that after demilitarisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: I want to get it quite clear. You only referred -- when talking about that Naser Oric may not have had no knowledge, you are only referring to this event and you would not make -- want to make a general statement about what Naser Oric knew or did not know?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In relation to Pirici, I think he didn't know. I think he was not familiar with the actual state of affairs at that time in as far is Pirici is concerned that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Judge Eser; I thank you, Judge Brydensholt. I don't have any questions for you, Witness, which basically means that your testimony ends here, comes to an end here. Before Madam Usher escorts you out of the courtroom, I should like to thank you on behalf of the Tribunal and also on behalf of Judge Brydensholt, Judge Eser, and myself for having come over to testify in this case against Naser Oric as a Defence witness. And I also wish to confirm to you that you will receive now all the assistance that you require to facilitate your return back home at the earliest. You have overstayed by a day, but that doesn't matter. Your testimony has been extremely important. So before you leave this courtroom, also on behalf of everyone, I would like to wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, while we await the entry of the next witness -- yes, I see Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I just have one thing related to the evidence of Mr. Malagic, and that is there was a Prosecution Exhibit P441 and we've tendered the transcript. And I believe that we just next an exhibit number --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So that would be in relation to V000-6036, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I believe that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this transcript which is described as not revised consisting two pages is being tendered by the Prosecution, received and marked as Prosecution Exhibit P441 point --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Point 1, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Dr. Mardel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome to this Tribunal. First of all I would like to apologise for having kept you waiting for so long, but the previous witness took a little bit longer than expected and his -- he was the kind of witness that we really couldn't ask to finish earlier. So my apologies to you and those of my two colleagues, Judge Brydensholt and Judge Eser. I am the Presiding Judge in this trial, and you are about to start giving evidence as one of the Defence witnesses. The procedure on this Tribunal requires that before you do so you enter a statement, solemn declaration, which is in lieu of an oath which you would have in domestic jurisdictions tantamount to a solemn declaration on your part, an undertaking on your part, that during the testimony you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is being handed to you by Madam Usher. Please read it out loud and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. Please make yourself comfortable. You will only be here for about 20 minutes today and then we will continue tomorrow. We will make every effort possible to try and finish tomorrow, but I am not in the position to guarantee you that for the time being. Mr. Jones, who is co-counsel in the Defence of Mr. Oric, will go first, and he will then be followed by Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Di Fazio, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, for cross-examination. The procedure is simple. I would imagine that you know what we are talking about. So, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And apologies from me, Dr. Mardel, for keeping you detained.

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, would you start by giving the court your full name?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL
utterances.text: Dr. Simon Nicholas Mardel.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL
utterances.text: 12th of February, 1957.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And is it correct that you currently live in Barrow-in-Furness?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL
utterances.text: Barrow-in-Furness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And you're married with two children?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And if you could confirm the following details: You're a medical doctor by profession, specialising in accident and emergency?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If I pause, it's for the interpreters. You have an M.Sc. in medical health and a diploma in tropical medicine and hygiene.

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And you've published numerous articles including on nutrition?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, before the war in Bosnia, you did NGO work in the field in Afghanistan, Liberia, and in Sudan?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And then since 1993 you worked regularly for the World Health Organisation, the WHO?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL
utterances.text: Periodically, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And do you know if your association with the WHO presents any impediment to you testifying publicly today?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any impediment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's do this in a more complete fashion. Have you been in contact with WHO about testifying here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I haven't. I know my office is aware of it. I've forewarned them that I might have to -- to come here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you have not received any communication from them? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes, Mr. Jones, carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, did your association --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, again. Let me interrupt you again. But I would still, out of an abundance of caution, suggest that if your witness is going to mention any individual from international organisations, that -- particularly his own, to indicate that and we'll have that -- those names mentioned in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, yes, Your Honour. Certainly for anyone else in WHO, I wasn't proposing to introduce any of their names. When it comes to members of the UNHCR and other agencies, we've actually already had copious reference to who was present in the areas which we covered, and it might be very cumbersome, in fact, to have to go in and out of private session whenever those people are mentioned. One has written a book about his experiences that has been mentioned during the testimony of other witnesses. So I would submit that actually for representatives of UNHCR that were there in the field that that's not necessary. Of course, I'm in your hands, and I'm happy to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Forget the person who wrote the book because he exposed himself and we can do nothing about it, but others I would still recommend that we are cautious in mentioning names because some of these people may still be in the field somewhere else and I would rather protect them than expose them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. And finally for clarification, that doesn't refer to members of UNPROFOR, that I can refer to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Those are common knowledge, anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: To you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Mardel, did you go to Bosnia in 1993?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In what capacity?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL
utterances.text: I was a field officer in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And is it right - and I presume I'm allowed to lead on this - that you were in Bosnia for four months in early 1993 and then again from October 1993 to April 1994?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And you were based in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you know of a place in Bosnia called Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you travel there in 1993?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to ask if the witness can be shown D232, Defence Exhibit 232.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the speakers please pause between the question and the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We're being reminded to pause.

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, firstly we see at the top it's the French embassy, Belgrade, for the urgent attention of ministry for humanitarian aid, details to be given to an organisation. And then from Dr. Simon Mardel --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Could you put the text on the ELMO and the witness can follow from there, please. The witness can follow on his screen, on his monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My question, firstly, is: Are you the author of this document?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Now, we see pretty much the second paragraph the heading: "Details of medical facilities and conditions in Srebrenica." And then: "See also summary of my visit to Konjevic Polje and Srebrenica 5 to 12 March, 1993, by Dr. Simon Mardel." Are those in fact the dates when you were in that area?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you know of a place called Cerska?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: When you were in Sarajevo before you went on this visit to Konjevic Polje, had you heard anything of Cerska?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL
utterances.text: I recall that there were -- an event had occurred in Cerska that was rumoured to be a massacre and that there was a large number of wounded as a result of so likely to be a large number of wounded as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So when you were in Sarajevo, was it your information that Cerska had fallen or was about to fall or could fall?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL
utterances.text: As I recall, it had -- it had fallen.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, I'm going to be referring to several passages of a book called: "Merry Christmas, Mr. Larry," by Larry Hollingworth. Are you familiar with this publication?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And when you came to The Hague did I ask you specifically to read chapter 9 of that book?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL
utterances.text: Yes, you did.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did you do so?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And is it broadly accurate, and we may come to any discrepancies, but as a description of your trip to Konjevic Polje in March 1993?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL
utterances.text: It's broadly accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, it's really in the interests of expediency that I'm going to take you to several passages and ask if they're accurate. I'm going to start with page 171, the second paragraph, and in fact we should go into private session because names are mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go to private session for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I see we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And is it correct that in Tuzla you were met by Major Allan Abraham of the 9th/10th [sic] Royal Lancers?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did that all occur on Friday, the 5th of March, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, continuing on that page there's reference to the Serbs delaying the convoy. It's page 171, second paragraph: "At Zvornik, however, we waited for hours." But would it be correct that you reached Konjevic Polje that evening, Friday, the 5th of March, by road?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In what vehicles was your group travelling?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL
utterances.text: We travelled in small armoured vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And which were you in among these vehicles?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL
utterances.text: The front one with General Morillon.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, we see, and it's maybe one of the discrepancies, page 173 towards the bottom. I see the third paragraph: "Naser Oric sent a vehicle to pick up the General. The rest of us struggled for hours." And further down, referring to one of the groups being cold and damp. "Simon, good soul that he is, dug out of his bergen some spare socks and a Gore Tex sleeping bag outer cover. "It was late when we entered Konjevici. None of us gave a thought to the Serb deadline of 2000 hours. The General was in the municipal building with Oric and the local authorities." Now, that suggests that you had to -- that you among others had to catch up with General Morillon. Is that correct.

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL
utterances.text: Yes. It suggests that when we were delayed at the barricade that he went through on his own. That sounds -- I recall something along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Were you in the same vehicle as the author of this work?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL
utterances.text: I was not -- I did not travel in the same vehicle as Larry, I'm pretty sure I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You mentioned being in a barricade. Was that -- do you recall your group encountering Bosnian men at some stage?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL
utterances.text: I recall the driver talking about what he could see and everyone could hear the driver. So he -- I recall him describing the barricade and I recall him -- the debate between the person in charge of the armoured vehicle and the driver, the to and fro discussion about whether or not and how to push through the barricade eventually, to push it to one side, possibly damaging the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: What was the barricade in fact made up of?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL
utterances.text: A -- great big tree trunks. Trees that were felled.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did you at that stage actually see the people who were being spoken to, the Bosnians who were at the barricade?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL
utterances.text: I do remember. I think we must have got out of the vehicles while waiting. I remember them looking a very dismal kind of bunch of people, of young men, poorly -- poorly clothed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did they resemble professional soldiers?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL
utterances.text: Not in my experience, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you recall anyone in your group at this stage saying We're here to see Oric or Take us to Oric or anything of that nature?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL
utterances.text: I don't recall that specific. It -- a meeting later occurred with -- with representatives, and, yeah, that seemed natural that there should be a delay while that was arranged or even a delay -- I can recall some discussion and delay as to whether or not we should -- we could even be allowed to enter. The men on the barricades, the local men, were quite anxious. There was some -- there was some problem with us -- with the concept of us actually entering, pushing through, with the vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Were those barricades in fact all that was between them and the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Or do you recall at any stage on the whole trip from Sarajevo to Konjevic Polje and the time when you were with General Morillon anyone mentioning a mission to see a named individual, a specific person, Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL
