utterances.text: I don't recall that, but I would not have been -- it was not my responsibility to be involved with -- with that. I was there to assess the wounded. That was my objective, and so I may not have paid much attention to -- to names and details.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, if we see again at page 173 of this book and it's the third paragraph. "The leader of the group was a tal, thin, mean, lean man. 'Why are you here,' He asked. 'Have you brought a convoy?' 'No,' we replied. 'We want to go and assess the situation in Cerska.' 'Cerska has fallen,' he said curtly." Now, my question: You said Cerska had already fallen. Do you recall there being any surprise when you arrived in Konjevic Polje, that Cerska had fallen or is that something you knew already?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL
utterances.text: This report conflicts with my memory and I'm going on -- I recall the morale of local staff that worked for us in Sarajevo about the situation -- there was a rumour in Sarajevo that Cerska had fallen, and I recall that rumour, if not fallen at least there had been -- there was a rumour of a massacre.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. And then just turning over the page, and we just have a few minutes, but I'm just going to deal with one area with three or four questions. Page 174, the fourth paragraph. "The conversation" -- and this is referring to this meeting which you've mentioned with the local authorities, as I think you've described them -- "the information then moved to medical matters. They discussed the situation in Konjevici and the Territorial Defence plight of Srebrenica. Simon then said, 'I would really like to get to Srebrenica.' This was no surprise statement; we all wanted to go to Srebrenica. Konjevici was a halfway house. But the Bosnians said, 'we can take you tonight.' I saw Simon's dark eyes light up. " 'No,' I said. 'It is important that he assesses here first.' 'No, Larry, no. It is good if he goes to Srebrenica,' said the General. 'No, General, he has not got the equipment and the initial requirement is here.'" Simon by this time had got his bergen on his back and was standing near the door. There was doubt about his feelings." Now, I just want to ask you, is that more or less how things transpired I mean, leaving aside the slightly flowery description, but there was this discussion and you decided to go to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL
utterances.text: I distinctly remember that our mission -- main mission that I understood was to assess the wounded from Cerska and that very quickly we were told that the most severely wounded had been taken over the hills to Srebrenica, which was a surprise to me that there was actually a route between what we considered as isolated enclaves. And they offered to take the doctor there, and I at that point said I would agree with that. And General Morillon supported that. And a discussion did occur between Larry and myself about Larry wanted me to stay and go in the morning and be fresh to do the medical assessment later in the day, and I said I was happier to travel through the night and I was well used to doing assessments or practicing medicine after being awake all night.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So in fact, just to tie this up, you did in fact leave that night, Friday, 5th of March, Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL
utterances.text: Yes. And in my -- I notice in one of my reports I even used the word "quickly" about leaving the meeting or quickly decided. And I would only have written that, given that meetings tend to go on a long time, I would have written that only if it was indeed quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: A final question on this. If someone among this group with whom you travelled into Konjevic Polje were you to say that you were around in Konjevic Polje the next day assessing the wounded on the Saturday, that would not be correct, would it?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: They would have got their facts seriously wrong if they were to state that?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL
utterances.text: Absolutely. I -- I know that -- you know, I can't -- I'll never forget a walk through the night and then going to bed in the early hours of the morning in the hospital and if I'd slept in Konjevic Polje, you know, I would have known about it. I would have remembered it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you very much?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's sufficient for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Shall we give this document an exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, this will become D777, and we will continue tomorrow, Dr. Mardel, in the morning at 9.00. And hopefully we won't keep you waiting. Do you think we will be able to finish tomorrow morning?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My estimate, given that we've made good use of this time, is two hours, two and a half maybe, maximum. I'm trusting that will be sufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Mr. Di Fazio? Roughly, of course, because we have barely started the direct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If it's about background material, medical conditions, and what this witness observed, life in Srebrenica, then my cross-examination will be brief in the extreme. If it's not, then I can't predict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So thanks to everyone for having overstayed with us for a few minutes. And we'll meet again tomorrow morning at 9.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 30th day of September, 2005, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.49 p.m.,
